metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Retrofit data centers hit structural weight limits before running out of electrical capacity, because liquid-cooled AI racks weigh far more than the buildings were designed to support.

Most enterprise data centers were engineered decades ago for air-cooled equipment distributed across standard racks. Liquid cooling systems add coolant, manifolds, and batteries that concentrate weight dramatically. When operators retrofit these older buildings for AI workloads, the raised floors or concrete slabs reach their load limits per square foot before the power infrastructure does. This inverts the traditional bottleneck. Projects fail on construction constraints rather than kilowatt constraints.

This matters because it decouples compute scaling from the electricity problem. A data center operator cannot simply upgrade transformers and buy more power if the building cannot physically support the weight. Retrofit projects become civil engineering problems first. The grid may have capacity, but the structure does not.

The metric does not cover how many existing data centers face this constraint, whether it affects new construction differently, or whether floor reinforcement is cheaper than building new. It isolates one decision point: the weight per square foot of what you want to install versus what the building will hold.
